label: Mock practice paper
source: School mock paper 2025–26; not an HKEAA paper
examNote: School-authored mock, not an official HKEAA paper. Formal exams require Chinese for the painting paper Part A; on this platform students may use guided self-check. Under 18 / age not confirmed: self-guide only — no AI marking.

aiPolicy.note: Under 18 or age not confirmed: use this checklist only — no AI trial marking.

instructions: Five questions; answer ONE question fully (Part A then Part B).
Part A: Art criticism (suggested 45 minutes, 20 marks) — describe, analyse, compare, interpret and evaluate both works.
Part B: Art making (suggested 3 h 15 min, 80 marks) — one two-dimensional work in any medium; submit sketches/notes and a ~50-word artist statement.
Read plate captions carefully; every artwork image carries source and licence.

questions.title: Q1: Cross-cultural comparison — Northern Song monumental landscape vs British Romantic industrial landscape
questions.compareFocus: Compare how both works use compositional scale, brushwork/facture, spatial layers and rhythmic movement (e.g. mountain pressing down on tiny travellers; rain, steam and the train’s rush) to express moving forward amid natural or historical forces; discuss differences in cultural ways of seeing and aesthetic orientation.

parts.label: Part A · Criticism
parts.prompt: Describe, analyse and compare the form and expression of plates (1a) and (1b), then interpret and evaluate both works. (20 marks)

selfCheck.text: I named media, subjects and the shared ‘advancing’ motif (mountain travel vs train in storm).
I framed (1a) as monumental landscape and (1b) as industrial-era dynamic landscape (Song stillness vs Romantic motion).
I compared scale/composition: giant peak / tiny travellers vs diagonal bridge and speed perspective.
I compared facture: raindrop/nail-head cun and dense ink vs thin glazes, impasto, rain and steam.
I compared atmosphere: quiet path-bound travel vs rush dissolved in light and vapour.
I linked Northern Song ‘learning from nature/heart’ and the idea of landscapes one may wander and dwell in.
I linked 19th-century British railways and Romantic awe/ambivalence toward nature and technology.
I gave an evidenced aesthetic judgement on how both elevate ‘advancing’ into a dialogue with force (reverent stillness vs modern turbulence).
My writing stays on visual evidence and the question’s focus — not biography alone.

markGuideSummary: Analyse: monumental press / tiny travellers vs diagonal speed / dissolved rain-steam; cun vs oily vapour.
Interpret: Song nature learning vs industrial Romanticism.
Evaluate: tie judgement to Advancing in the Wind.

parts.label: Part B · Creation
parts.prompt: Create a two-dimensional work on the theme Advancing in the Wind. (80 marks)
parts.hint: Transform Part A insights (pressing scale / speed; tiny advance / steam-light; solid–void layers) into a personal response to journey, weather or change. Submit sketches/notes on the support. Write a ~50-word statement linking intent to Part A.
parts.themePrompt: Make a two-dimensional work on Advancing in the Wind. Transform Part A visual language (pressing scale / speed; tiny advance / steam-light; solid–void layers) into a personal statement about journey, weather or historical change.
mediaConstraints: Any 2D medium (ink, watercolour, acrylic, mixed media, etc.)
Must remain a flat/two-dimensional work (this paper's Part B)
Encourage visible wind/rain/vapour atmosphere and a sense of advance or journey

checklist.text: Composition shows a clear path of movement or scale tension (e.g. diagonal advance, pressing distance vs near figure).
Medium supports the idea (e.g. dense dots/short cun in distance; slanted washes or flying white in foreground).
Theme Advancing in the Wind is readable in the image, not only in the title.
Sketches/process notes are included with transfer points from Part A.
~50-word artist statement links intent to Part A criticism.
At least one visual idea is explicitly transferred from plate (1a) or (1b).
